notes: Large Commercial Court forum non conveniens judgment on insurance coverage; jurisdiction and applicable-law analysis are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Forum conveniens in Sun Life professional liability coverage dispute

statutes_considered.title: Council Regulation (EC) No 44/2001 on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters

key_facts: Insurers on a global financial institution professional liability policy issued proceedings in the Commercial Court seeking negative declarations that a claim by Sun Life for UK past-business-review costs was excluded by a warranty and/or late notification.
Sun Life UK and Sun Life Canada commenced parallel proceedings in Ontario seeking indemnity and punitive damages, alleging forum shopping.
The dispute arose from Sun Life UK's regulatory dealings with the PIA/FSA and costs of reviewing past business after a focus visit in 2000.
Sun Life applied to stay the English proceedings in favour of Ontario on forum non conveniens grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to stay English proceedings against an English-domiciled defendant and to set aside service out of the jurisdiction on the Canadian parent company.
enrichment.outcome: Stay refused and permission to serve Sun Life Canada out of the jurisdiction upheld; England held to be the clearly more appropriate forum.
enrichment.ratio: Despite post-UGIC debate over Article 2 of the Brussels Regulation, Re Harrods remained binding authority allowing forum non conveniens review where the competing forum is outside the EU; on the facts of a UK-regulatory insurance coverage dispute governed by arguable English or Ontario law, England was the more appropriate forum because the central evidence concerned Sun Life UK's dealings with the FSA/PIA, most witnesses and documents were in England, and Ontario punitive damages were not realistically in play.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 of the Brussels Regulation precludes a stay in favour of a non-member state court
Whether Re Harrods survives Universal General Insurance Co v Group Josi Reinsurance
Which forum is clearly and distinctly more appropriate for trial
Whether the policy is governed by English or Ontario law
Whether Ontario section 129 relief from forfeiture and punitive damages materially favoured Canada
Whether negative declaration proceedings were improper forum shopping

notes: Summary judgment on Law Society intervention challenge after SDT dishonesty findings; procedural history and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Summary dismissal of challenge to Law Society intervention
key_facts: The Law Society intervened in Paul Simms's practice in February 2002 on suspicion of dishonesty following inspections of the Bower Cotton Partnership.
Six claimants, including partners and salaried partners, sought an order requiring withdrawal of the intervention under paragraph 6(4) of Schedule 1 to the Solicitors Act 1974.
Mr Simms was subsequently found by the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal to have been dishonest in relation to bogus transactions, conflicts, money laundering failures and related misconduct.
The intervention proceedings had been adjourned pending the SDT hearing and were resumed after findings of dishonesty were made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim and application for summary dismissal under CPR 24.2 after SDT findings of dishonesty.
enrichment.outcome: Claim summarily dismissed; Mr Simms ordered to pay the Law Society's costs on an indemnity basis and the second and third claimants ordered to pay costs up to June 2002 on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: In proceedings to terminate a Law Society intervention, the court decides on all evidence available at the time of hearing; SDT findings of dishonesty may be treated like convictions and, even pending appeal, leave no real prospect that the Society lacked reason to suspect dishonesty at the time of intervention; where no effective relief beyond a declaration would remain, continuation to trial is futile.
legal_issues: Whether the claim should await the outcome of Mr Simms's appeal against SDT findings
Whether SDT dishonesty findings defeat the challenge to the intervention
What relief, if any, remained available to the claimants
Whether the second and third claimants were proper parties liable for costs
index_terms: Office for the Supervision of Solicitors
linked_authorities: Buckley v The Law Society (No 2) [1984] 1 WLR 1101
Wilson Smith v The Law Society (unreported, 21 February 2000)
Virdi v The Law Society (unreported, 30 March 2000)

notes: Statutory construction appeal on street works cost sharing; Code of Practice stages C2-C4 analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Allowable costs of Appendix C4 detailed utility estimates

statutes_considered.title: New Roads and Street Works Act 1991
Street Works (Sharing of Costs of Works) Regulations 1992

key_facts: BT claimed £684.14 from Gwynedd Council for preparing a detailed client estimate after major bridge works on the A494 potentially affected BT apparatus.
The parties followed the Code of Practice procedures through preliminary inquiries (C2) and draft scheme/budget estimates (C3) before Gwynedd submitted final design details triggering the C4 stage.
Gwynedd refused payment, arguing C4 estimate preparation fell within the excluded initial planning costs under Regulation 2(2)(a).
The county court judge held the first C4 detailed estimate was an allowable cost and made a declaration to that effect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Manchester County Court on construction of allowable costs under the 1991 Act and 1992 Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; preparation of the first detailed C4 estimate following C2 and C3 stages held to be an allowable cost.
enrichment.ratio: Allowable costs under section 85 and Regulation 2(2) are not limited to physical execution works but exclude only the initial set of plans and estimates; where the full Code of Practice route is followed, the C3 budget estimate is the initial set and the first C4 detailed estimate is a further estimate for which the undertaker may charge, whereas if C2/C3 are foreshortened the first C4 estimate is itself initial and not chargeable.
legal_issues: Whether C4 detailed estimate preparation costs are allowable costs
Meaning of initial set of plans and estimates in Regulation 2(2)(a)
Relationship between the Regulations and the Code of Practice Appendix C stages
Whether paragraph 9.2 of the Code excludes all C4 planning and liaison costs
index_terms: New Roads and Street Works Act 1991

notes: Construction site tripping accident; liability apportionment and quantum on loss of earnings are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Tripping on floor studs at warehouse construction site
key_facts: Michael Humpheryes, a self-employed steel erector, tripped on resin-fixed floor studs protruding about five inches in a warehouse bulk storage area at Greenford in October 1999.
Nedcon UK had subcontracted shelving installation to Storage Engineering Services, which had fixed the studs that morning without cordoning off the area or posting warnings.
The claimant injured his right knee and shoulder, did not return to heavy steel-erecting work, and claimed damages for injury and loss of earnings.
Site supervisors gave unreliable evidence about prior warnings, barriering and a separate cherry-picker incident.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of liability and quantum in the Queen's Bench Division following denial of negligence and breach of statutory duty.
enrichment.outcome: Both Nedcon and SES held liable under Regulations 5 and 15 and in negligence, with liability apportioned two-thirds to Nedcon and one-third to SES; contributory negligence rejected; damages awarded including £14,000 general damages and past/future loss of earnings.
enrichment.ratio: Where studs created an obvious tripping hazard near a doorway used by other trades, both the main subcontractor controlling the works and the installing subcontractor retained sufficient control under regulation 4(2) to owe duties under Regulations 5 and 15; failure to barrier the area or warn was a breach and not excused by the claimant's failure to look at the ground when no warning existed.
legal_issues: Which defendant controlled the construction site for the purposes of regulation 4(2)
Whether Regulations 5 and 15 were breached by leaving studs unmarked and uncordoned
Whether the claimant was contributorily negligent
Quantum of general damages, loss of earnings, pension loss and care

confidence.notes: Findings on liability, apportionment and principal quantum headings are clear. Detailed medical and accounting evidence is summarised at trial level.

notes: Short Attorney General's reference on unduly lenient section 18 sentence; facts and substituted sentence are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: unduly lenient knife wounding sentence increased
key_facts: The offender, aged 25, pleaded guilty to wounding with intent, burglary and common assault arising from events in Leeds in 2003 while on bail.

After a dispute with Donna Abbott he assaulted her with a cigarette lighter, then after a neighbour intervened feigned a handshake and slashed the neighbour's face with a knife causing facial cuts requiring stitches.
He had previous convictions including two section 20 GBH offences for which he received 30 months' imprisonment in 2000.
The recorder imposed consecutive sentences totalling three and a half years, including only 18 months for the section 18 offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; section 18 sentence increased from 18 months to three years, making a total sentence of five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Even where consecutive sentences are properly imposed for separate offences, the court must give proper effect to the seriousness of a section 18 knife attack carried out by subterfuge after an sustained assault on a Good Samaritan; a sentence below three years for the section 18 offence was unduly lenient notwithstanding mitigation and totality considerations.
legal_issues: Whether the section 18 sentence was unduly lenient taken alone
Whether totality justified the lenient section 18 term when consecutive sentences were imposed
Appropriate bracket for knife wounding with intent following Attorney General's Reference No 18 of 2002
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 18 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr App R (S) 35

confidence.notes: Facts, prior convictions, original sentence and substituted sentence are all clearly stated in a short judgment.

notes: Visitor jurisdiction and natural justice in university degree termination appeal; procedural unfairness finding balanced against futility on merits.

enrichment.short_title: Visitor appeal procedure and Cranfield degree termination
key_facts: Mr Varma's registration on an MSc course at Cranfield University was terminated for failure to maintain satisfactory academic progress after poor examination results in 2000-2001.
Internal university appeals failed and he appealed to the Duke of Kent as Visitor, who appointed a circuit judge as commissary to investigate and advise before dismissing the petition.
The claimant challenged the visitorial process by judicial review, arguing unlawful delegation and failure to disclose the commissary's advice before the final decision.
Collins J held the commissary procedure lawful but that fairness required prior disclosure of the advice, though relief was refused because the appeal would inevitably have failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Royal Visitor's dismissal of a university student's appeal against termination of registration.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; claimant ordered to pay 75 per cent of the University's costs subject to legal aid protection.
enrichment.ratio: A visitor may appoint a lawyer of standing to conduct a fair investigation and tender advice without unlawfully delegating the visitor's decision, but where the visitor's decision is final and not court-reviewable on merits, natural justice requires the appellant to see and comment on the advice on limited grounds before the visitor decides; relief may nonetheless be refused where no representation could have affected the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether the Duke of Kent unlawfully delegated his visitatorial decision-making function
Whether judicial review lies against a visitor acting within jurisdiction
Whether the claimant should have seen the commissary's report before the visitor's final decision
Whether any procedural defect warranted quashing the visitor's decision

R v Lord President of the Privy Council, ex p Page [1993] AC 682
Patel v Bradford University Senate [1978] 1 WLR 1488
Philips v Bury (1694) Holt KB 715

notes: Composite Attorney General's reference judgment reviewing six sentences; framework and individual outcomes are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General review of six unduly lenient sentences

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard six Attorney General references together and restated that intervention requires manifest undue leniency or error of principle, not mere disagreement with a trial judge's exceptional discretion.
Thomas McInerney's ISSP supervision order for robbery was upheld after positive post-sentence progress despite mobile-phone robbery guidelines favouring custody.

Adele McLean's eight-month sentence for robbery and Daniel Burgess's community order for section 18 wounding were treated differently: McLean's reference made no order after post-release rehabilitation, Burgess's sentence was replaced with two-and-a-half years.

AC's indecent assault sentences on his stepdaughter were increased to two years with extended licence; Surinder and Bhupinder Lehal's suspended sentences for perverting the course of justice were upheld.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's references under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 reviewing six Crown Court sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted on all references; no order in McInerney, McLean and Lehal references; Burgess sentenced to two-and-a-half years' imprisonment; AC's custodial term increased to two years with extended licence periods.
enrichment.ratio: The Attorney General's reference jurisdiction preserves trial judges' exceptional sentencing discretion and requires manifest undue leniency before intervention; where a community sentence for robbery or wounding may initially appear too lenient, post-sentence progress and lack of public-interest in recall may justify no order, but a manifestly unduly lenient section 18 community sentence must be replaced with a substantial custodial term.
legal_issues: When the Court of Appeal should interfere with unduly lenient sentences
Role of post-sentence reports in robbery and community sentence references
Appropriate levels for section 18 wounding with intent and indecent assault on a child
Whether suspended sentences for perverting the course of justice were lawful and exceptional
Whether judges may impose programme conditions on extended licence at sentencing

notes: Planning appeal under section 288; countryside policy and abandonment arguments clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Planning refusal for fire-damaged countryside dwelling rebuild
key_facts: The claimants owned Brickyard Farm, a dwelling in open countryside near Burbage, Leicestershire, which was badly damaged by vandalism and fire in August 2000 after earlier permission for alterations subject to a no-demolition condition.
Only part of the structure remained standing and the local planning authority refused a 2003 application to rebuild, treating the proposal as a new countryside dwelling contrary to local plan policy.
An inspector dismissed the appeal, concluding the works would effectively construct a new house in the countryside.
The claimants challenged the decision on abandonment and Article 1 Protocol 1 grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; inspector's decision upheld and claimant ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs of £3,410.
enrichment.ratio: It was not Wednesbury unreasonable for the inspector to treat the severely fire-damaged remains as incapable of residential use and the proposal as effectively a new dwelling conflicting with countryside housing policies; refusal of planning permission did not engage Article 1 Protocol 1 because it deprived the owners only of a hope of permission, not of possession or peaceful enjoyment.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector irrationally treated physical condition as determinative of abandonment
Whether the use of the dwelling had been abandoned
Whether Policy RES10 permitted a replacement dwelling in the circumstances
Whether refusal of planning permission breached Article 1 of Protocol 1
linked_authorities: Hughes v Secretary of State for the Environment [2000] 1 PLR 76

confidence.notes: Grounds of challenge, inspector reasoning and dismissal on both planning and human rights grounds are clearly set out.

notes: Renewed permission application on Arbitration Act 1996 section 28 delay; judge's discretion analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Delay in challenging arbitrator's fees under section 28
key_facts: United Tyre Company challenged fees totalling about £44,900 plus VAT charged by arbitrator Mr Born after a complex commercial arbitration in which the respondent largely succeeded.
The respondent paid the fees under reservation in December 2001 and pursued detailed correspondence seeking breakdowns before issuing a section 28 application in May 2003.
The parties agreed a preliminary issue whether delay barred any adjustment of the arbitrator's fees.
The judge held that despite substantial delay and no prejudice to the arbitrator, the claimant remained entitled to have the fees considered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against a preliminary issue decision in Mercantile Court proceedings under section 28 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; claimant held entitled to determination of whether the arbitrator's fees were excessive.
enrichment.ratio: Section 28(3) contains no fixed time limit and requires the court to ask whether repayment is reasonable in all the circumstances; unreasonable delay is an important but not automatic bar, especially where the paying party put the arbitrator on notice of challenge, continued negotiations, and no prejudice is shown.
legal_issues: Whether delay in bringing a section 28 application automatically bars relief
Whether lack of prejudice to the arbitrator is relevant once delay is established
How section 1(a)'s expedition principle applies to fee challenges
Whether the judge erred in treating early notice of challenge as a factor favouring relief

confidence.notes: Chronology, statutory test and refusal of permission are clearly explained. Merits of the underlying fee challenge were not decided.
